meta.description: Daily tracking state for F-1/SEVP/DS-2019 policy monitoring, focused on relevance to a Virginia Tech student who may need an extra semester to finish their degree.

items.title: DHS Final Rule: Fixed Time Period of Admission & Extension of Stay (ends Duration of Status) for F, J, I nonimmigrants
items.summary: DHS published a final rule (doc. 2026-14439) on Jul 17, 2026, ending open-ended Duration of Status for F-1 students, effective Sep 15, 2026. Students get a fixed 'Admit Until Date' capped at 4 years (24 months for language programs); anyone needing more time must file Form I-539 (Extension of Stay) with USCIS in addition to the existing DSO SEVIS extension -- the I-539 EOS filing fee is reported as $420 filed online / $470 by paper. A timely-filed EOS gives up to 240 days of authorized stay while pending. The rule also shortens the F-1 post-completion grace period from 60 to 30 days for anyone who travels/re-enters or gets an EOS approval after the effective date. Students already in D/S status who remain continuously in the U.S. without leaving/re-entering keep transition protections, but only up to a hard outside cap of Nov 14, 2030 (4 years + 60-day grace period measured from the Sep 15, 2026 effective date). DHS has discretion to postpone, until as late as Sep 14, 2028, implementation of the specific provisions restricting mid-program school transfers, changes in educational objective (major/level), and progression to same- or lower-level programs, if DHS determines full implementation isn't feasible by the Sep 15, 2026 effective date -- this discretionary postponement option applies only to those specific transfer/education-level provisions, not to the core fixed-admission-period change itself. As a major rule, it is also subject to Congressional Review Act review: Congress has a 60-day window after the rule is reported to introduce a joint resolution of disapproval, which -- if enacted -- would void the rule and bar a substantially similar rule absent new legislation; as of this run no such resolution has been reported as introduced. USCIS will publish revised editions of Form I-539 and Form I-765 effective Sep 15, 2026, aligned to the new fixed-admission-period process -- the current 08/28/24 edition of Form I-539 will still be accepted if postmarked or e-filed before Sep 15, 2026, but rejected on/after that date (no grace period), after which only the new 09/15/26 edition is accepted. On Aug 18, 2026, the anticipated legal challenge became a real lawsuit: NAFSA, the Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, and other higher-ed/labor groups filed a complaint and motion for preliminary injunction against the rule in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, seeking to stay and vacate it (or at minimum block its enforcement against plaintiffs and their members) before the Sep 15, 2026 effective date -- see new item 'lawsuit-vs-ds-rule-2026-08' for full details.
items.notes: Update 2026-08-19 (sixth check): the lawsuit NAFSA/Presidents' Alliance had been preparing since late July was actually filed on Aug 18, 2026 (tracked separately as new item 'lawsuit-vs-ds-rule-2026-08'); no ruling on the preliminary injunction motion yet. Also found today that Cranwell International Center now maintains a dedicated 'Duration of Status Updates' page (international.vt.edu/duration_of_status.html), separate from and more specific than the general immigration_updates.html page found in prior runs -- it confirms Cranwell is reviewing the final rule, tells students to keep submitting extension/CPT/OPT/reduced-course-load/degree-level-change requests through the IntlHokies Portal as normal, and directs D/S-specific questions to international@vt.edu. No Congressional Review Act disapproval resolution had been introduced as of this run. SEVP stakeholder webinar remains scheduled for Mon, Aug 31, 2026, 2-3pm ET per Study in the States.

items.title: NEW: Coalition sues DHS, seeks preliminary injunction to block/vacate the D/S-ending final rule before Sep 15
items.source: Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration / NAFSA (press release); press reporting
items.summary: On Aug 18, 2026, a coalition -- NAFSA: Association of International Educators, the Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts (AICUM), the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), the Graduate Labor Organization (AFT Local 6516), the UAW, UAW Local 2322, and The NewsGuild-CWA -- filed a complaint and motion for preliminary injunction in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts challenging DHS's July 17, 2026 final rule that ends Duration of Status for F, J, and I nonimmigrants. Plaintiffs argue the rule is arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act and warn of severe economic and academic harm -- reduced international enrollment, weakened university finances, and loss of talent in critical fields -- and ask the court to stay and vacate the rule, or at minimum enjoin its enforcement against plaintiffs and their members, before it takes effect Sep 15, 2026. This is the first concrete legal challenge to the rule; NAFSA had signaled since late July it was preparing litigation (see item 'd-s-final-rule') but no complaint had been filed until now. Directly relevant to a student weighing an extra semester: if the court grants a stay or injunction before Sep 15, the fixed-admission-period/I-539 Extension-of-Stay requirement could be paused or delayed for some or all F-1 students; if the motion is denied or not decided in time, the rule proceeds as scheduled on Sep 15.
items.notes: First identified today via multiple simultaneous press reports (Forbes/Stuart Anderson, STAT News, Boston Globe, ICEF Monitor, The PIE News) all describing the same Aug 18, 2026 filing in D. Mass., corroborated by the plaintiff coalition's own press release. Targeted searches on federal-court domains (mad.uscourts.gov, courtlistener.com, pacermonitor.com) did not surface a matching docket entry in today's search results, so this is not yet elevated to 'Confirmed (official)' -- a specific case/docket number circulating in some AI-summarized search results could not be independently verified against a primary court source today and is deliberately omitted pending confirmation. Will keep searching for the official court docket and for any ruling on the preliminary injunction motion, which is the actionable trigger for whether the Sep 15, 2026 effective date actually holds.

items.title: NEW: USCIS Interim Final Rule enabling mandatory electronic filing (e-Filing) -- covers I-539/I-765 among forms in scope
items.summary: USCIS published an interim final rule (91 FR 51924, doc. 2026-16313), effective Aug 11, 2026, giving USCIS authority to require mandatory electronic filing (e-filing) of certain benefit requests. The rule itself does not immediately force any specific form online -- USCIS may only mandate e-filing for a form once that form has been available for e-filing for at least 180 days, and must give at least 60 days' advance public notice before a mandate for a specific form/filing circumstance takes effect. It does not affect petitions already pending. Secondary coverage lists an initial set of roughly 22 forms USCIS is expected to phase toward mandatory e-filing, reportedly including I-129, I-130, N-400, I-90, I-131, and -- notably -- I-539 (Extension/Change of Nonimmigrant Status) and I-765 (Employment Authorization). This directly matters for F-1 students who will need to file Form I-539 for an Extension of Stay (EOS) once the Sep 15, 2026 fixed-admission-period rule takes effect, and for I-765 OPT/STEM OPT applicants: if/when USCIS issues the required 60-day notice mandating e-filing for these forms, paper filing could stop being accepted for them. Public comments on the interim final rule are open through Oct 13, 2026.
items.notes: First identified 2026-08-18 via a general OPT/CPT news sweep, then confirmed directly against the Federal Register document and a matching official USCIS newsroom alert ('USCIS To Require Electronic Filing of Forms: Strengthening National Security'). Rechecked 2026-08-19 (second check): still no 60-day mandate notice for any specific form (including I-539/I-765) has been published -- only the enabling framework and the interim final rule itself. Will track for the first form-specific mandate notice, which would be the actionable trigger for students filing extension-of-stay or OPT paperwork.

items.title: DHS regulatory review of OPT / STEM OPT (RIN 1653-AA97) — no NPRM published yet
items.summary: DHS confirmed in a Jan 9, 2026 letter it is re-evaluating the scope and duration of OPT and STEM OPT, with a rulemaking entry (RIN 1653-AA97, titled 'Practical Training') in the Unified Regulatory Agenda covering worker protection, fraud prevention, national security, and SEVP oversight goals. As of this run, no Notice of Proposed Rulemaking has been published in the Federal Register. Secondary sources continue to cite the government's own unified agenda as listing an NPRM target of February 2027 for this rule. OPT and STEM OPT remain fully operational and unchanged today. Reconfirmed today via reginfo.gov's own RIN 1653-AA97 entry, which describes the proposed rule's purpose in DHS's own words -- to 'better align practical training to the goals and objectives of the program' and 'address fraud and national security concerns, protect U.S. workers from being displaced by foreign nationals, and enhance [SEVP's] capacity to oversee the program.' Relevant because many students planning an extra semester are also relying on post-completion OPT/STEM OPT timing.
items.notes: No OPT/STEM OPT NPRM has been published as of 2026-08-19 (sixth check). No material change from prior run; reginfo.gov was reachable and reconfirmed the same docket entry.

items.title: ICE/HSI announces nationwide OPT fraud crackdown: 10,000+ students linked to 'suspect employers'
items.source: Press reporting of ICE/HSI press conference (Acting Director Todd Lyons)
items.summary: At a May 12, 2026 press conference, Acting ICE Director Todd Lyons and Acting HSI Associate Director John Condon announced that federal investigators had identified more than 10,000 F-1/STEM OPT students linked to 'highly suspect employers' -- among the top 25 OPT-employing companies reviewed. HSI site visits across eight states (TX, VA, GA, IL, NY, NJ, NC, FL) reportedly found empty buildings, locked doors, residential addresses listed as worksites, shell companies, and offshore payroll/HR arrangements; in one Northern Texas case an employer claimed 500 OPT students but had only 3 actual employees on site. Lyons called it 'only the tip of the iceberg.' Directly relevant to any student counting on post-completion OPT/STEM OPT -- especially under an extended timeline -- since it signals intensified employer-level scrutiny and potential SEVIS/EAD complications for students whose employer gets flagged, even if the student did nothing wrong.
items.notes: Still widely reported by many independent outlets describing the same May 12, 2026 press conference. Rechecked 2026-08-19 (sixth check): targeted site:ice.gov / site:dhs.gov searches again surfaced only general/older SEVP fraud material (a Feb 2024 STEM OPT fraud broadcast message, an archived 2020 arrests release, and a Northern Virginia employer site-visit release) -- none matching the specific '10,000+ students' / May 12 press-conference claim. Both domains remain reachable and return other current, relevant SEVP material, so this continues to look like a genuine gap in official coverage of this specific number rather than a source-access problem. Will keep searching for a matching official statement or follow-on enforcement actions.

items.title: USCIS Policy Alert PA-2026-05: officers may deny incomplete filings without issuing an RFE/NOID first
items.summary: Effective Aug 5, 2026, USCIS updated Policy Manual guidance so adjudicators may, at their discretion, deny a benefit request lacking required initial evidence or failing to establish eligibility without first issuing an RFE or NOID, and may set RFE response deadlines shorter than the prior 12-week norm (the 14-day international-mail grace period was also eliminated). Directly relevant to F-1 students filing Form I-539 (Extension of Stay) or I-765 under the new fixed-admission-period regime: an incomplete EOS package can now be denied outright with no chance to cure. This compounds with the new mandatory e-filing framework (see new item above), since incomplete or improperly formatted e-filed packages would carry the same denial risk.
items.notes: No changes found today (sixth check). Confirmed via the official USCIS newsroom alert and the underlying Policy Alert PA-2026-05 PDF, which updates USCIS-PM E.6, E.9, and E.10, effective for requests pending or filed on/after Aug 5, 2026.

items.title: SEVP Broadcast Message BCM 2608-01: DSOs warned on CPT authorization liability, increased scrutiny
items.summary: On Aug 12, 2026, SEVP issued Broadcast Message 2608-01, 'Reminder of Liability for DSOs Regarding CPT Authorization,' to every PDSO/DSO at SEVP-certified schools. SEVP says it has observed a rise in Curricular Practical Training (CPT) authorizations that do not meet regulatory requirements -- specifically CPT not constituting an integral part of an established curriculum -- and is increasing scrutiny of CPT approvals; the message states DSOs should only authorize CPT where its absence 'would make the attainment of a degree an impossibility.' The message does not change the CPT regulation itself and DHS's July D/S final rule separately stated it 'does not prohibit or eliminate Day-1 CPT' and 'does not make substantive changes to CPT.' But it signals stepped-up enforcement: schools found authorizing CPT improperly risk investigation and loss of SEVP certification. Washington State University's Aug 7, 2026 international-office advisory announced ISSS there will stop approving full-time CPT during the academic year starting Spring 2027, except for programs with an explicit mandatory-internship curriculum requirement -- an early example of a university preemptively tightening its own CPT approval practices. No indication yet that Virginia Tech's Cranwell International Center has announced a similar change; VT's CPT page still describes standard part-time/full-time CPT eligibility rules with no dated policy update.
items.notes: No regulatory text has changed -- this remains a compliance/enforcement reminder, not a rulemaking. Rechecked 2026-08-19: no new VT-specific CPT update found (VT's international.vt.edu/employment/cpt.html still shows standard, unchanged CPT guidance), though VT's new Duration of Status Updates page (see item 'd-s-final-rule') does note students should keep submitting CPT requests via IntlHokies as normal. No new facts found today beyond prior runs.

items.title: 30 Senators press State Dept (Rubio) to clear F/M/J student visa interview backlog before fall term
items.source: Office of Sen. Alex Padilla (official press release) / press reporting
items.summary: On Aug 11, 2026, 30 U.S. Senators led by Sen. Alex Padilla sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying 'no timely visa appointments are available for students at some embassies and consulates' during peak season, and asking the State Department to restore priority to F, M, and J visa interviews, extend interview waivers for vetted returning students, and boost consular staffing before fall term starts. The letter gives State roughly 30 days to respond to 10 questions -- a deadline around mid-September 2026, after most fall terms have already begun. Not a rule change, but directly relevant to any F-1 student (including someone on an extended timeline) who needs to obtain a new visa stamp or renew one to travel and re-enter, especially once the Sep 15, 2026 D/S-to-fixed-admission-period transition takes effect.
items.notes: No State Department response found yet (not due until ~mid-September 2026, fifth check today). Will keep tracking for a State Department response or a change in interview-scheduling practice.

items.title: Reported $100,000 fee under consideration for OPT / post-completion work authorization
items.source: Press reporting (Forbes, Bloomberg, ICEF Monitor, The PIE News, Higher Ed Dive)
items.summary: Multiple outlets report the administration is weighing a $100,000 fee applicable to OPT employment authorization (and by extension STEM OPT), modeled on the now-struck-down $100,000 H-1B fee proclamation. As of this run, no signed proclamation or DHS proposed rule/fee schedule has been reported for an OPT fee -- unlike the H-1B fee, which was signed via proclamation on Sep 19, 2025 and then struck down by a federal judge on Jun 8, 2026. Immigration attorneys quoted say an OPT fee is unlikely to survive legal challenge absent Congressional authorization, citing that H-1B precedent plus a Jul 24, 2026 appellate rejection of the administration's appeal. Who would pay (student/university/employer) remains unresolved. Directly relevant to students weighing an extra semester who are also counting on post-completion OPT/STEM OPT to work in the U.S. afterward.
items.notes: Still no DHS/USCIS/.gov statement, proposed rule, or signed proclamation found confirming or denying this as of 2026-08-19 (sixth check today). No proclamation has been signed. Reporting continues to cite the H-1B fee litigation as the key legal headwind to an OPT-fee proclamation surviving challenge; the DHS 2026 Unified Agenda still lists the related 'Practical Training' rulemaking (RIN 1653-AA97) with an NPRM target of Feb 2027, not a standalone OPT fee action.

items.title: NAFSA/JB International report: fall 2026 international enrollment projected to fall ~9.5% (~111,000 students) amid visa crackdown
items.source: NAFSA: Association of International Educators / JB International (research report, press reporting)
items.summary: A report released Aug 11, 2026 by NAFSA and research firm JB International, based on institutional responses to IIE's Spring 2026 Snapshot survey, projects fall 2026 international enrollment at U.S. colleges will fall about 9.5% (secondary sources cite figures ranging ~111,000-112,000 fewer students), citing declining applications, visa-appointment bottlenecks, and newly restrictive immigration policy (including the D/S final rule) as converging headwinds. Estimated economic impact: ~$3.4 billion in lost local spending and ~39,000-40,000 jobs. Inside Higher Ed's coverage adds that 63% of surveyed institutions anticipate an enrollment decline for 2026-2027 (vs. 11% expecting an increase, 26% expecting stable numbers). This is a research/economic-impact projection rather than a new rule -- it is being tracked here as evidence of how seriously the sector expects the policy changes above to bite, which is relevant context (not itself an actionable status change) for a student weighing an extra semester.
items.notes: This is a private-association economic/enrollment projection, not a government policy claim, so there is no .gov document that would ever 'confirm' it in the same sense as the other items -- it is tracked as 'Reported, unconfirmed' per the tracker's default schema, but readers should treat that label as 'not a government-verifiable fact' rather than 'possibly false.' No change in the core finding today (sixth check); secondary reporting today reiterates spring 2026 international enrollment fell ~20% year-over-year, consistent with the fall projection.
